source_text: Ὁ τοίνυν Κέλσος, οὐ γενόμενος δίκαιος ἐξεταστὴς τῶν λεγομένων παρ᾿ Αἰγυπτίοις ἑτέρως καὶ παρ᾿ Ἑβραίοις ἄλλως, ἀλλὰ προκαταληφθεὶς ὡς ὑπὸ φιλτέρων τῶν Αἰγυπτίων, τοῖς μὲν ἀδικήσασι τοὺς ξένους συγκατέθετο ὡς ἀληθέσι τοὺς δ᾿ ἀδικηθέντας Ἑβραίους στασιάζοντας εἶπε τὴν Αἴγυπτον καταλελοιπέναι, οὐχ ὁρῶν τίνα τρόπον οὐ δύναται τηλικοῦτο στασιῶδες πλῆθος Αἰγυπτίων. ἀρχὴν ἔχον τὴν στάσιν, γενέσθαι ἔθνος ἅμα τῷ στασιάζειν καὶ τὴν διάλεκτον ἀμεῖβον, ἵν᾿ οἱ τέως τῇ Αἰγυπτίων φωνῇ χρώμενοι αἰφνίδιον τὴν Ἑβραίων διάλεκτον συμπληρῶσιν. Ἔστω δὲ καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν καταλιπόντας αὐτοὺς τὴν Αἴγυπτον μεμισηκέναι καὶ τὴν σύντροφον φωνήν· πῶς οὖν τὸ μετὰ τοῦτο οὐχὶ μᾶλλον τῇ Σύρων ἐχρῶντο διαλέκτῳ ἢ τῇ Φοινίκων, ἀλλὰ τὴν Ἑβραΐδα ἑτέραν παρ᾿ ἀμφοτέρας συνεστήσαντο; τοῦτο δέ μοι βούλεται ὁ λόγος συνάγειν ὅτι ψεῦδος τὸ Αἰγυπτίους τὸ γένος ὄντας τινὰς ἐστασιακέναι πρὸς Αἰγυπτίους καὶ τὴν Αἴγυπτον καταλελοιπέναι καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν Παλαιστίνην ἐληλυθέναι τήν τε νῦν καλουμένην Ἰουδαίαν ᾠκηκέναι. Ἑβραίων γὰρ καὶ διάλεκτος πάτριος πρὸ τῆς εἰς Αἴγυπτον αὐτῶν καθόδου ἦν, καὶ Ἑβραϊκὰ γράμματα ἕτερα παρὰ τὰ Αἰγυπτίων ἦν, οἷς Μωϋσῆς χρησάμενος ἔγραψε τὰς παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις πεπιστευμένας εἶναι ἱερὰς πέντε βίβλους.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore Celsus, not having become a just examiner of the things said by Egyptians in one way and by Hebrews in another, but having been preconceived as by the lovers of the Egyptians, to those who did wrong to the foreigners he assented as to true things, and to the wronged Hebrews, who were rebelling, he said that they left Egypt, not seeing in what way such a large rebellious crowd of Egyptians could not have come into being, having the rebellion as a beginning, and becoming a nation at the same time as rebelling, and changing their dialect, so that those who were until then using the Egyptian voice might suddenly fill up the Hebrew dialect. But let it be, for the sake of hypothesis, that they, having left Egypt, hated it and the accompanying voice; how then did they not rather use the Syrian dialect after that, or the Phoenician, but established the Hebrew one, different from both? This, however, my argument wants to gather, that it is a falsehood that some Egyptians, being of the genus, rebelled against the Egyptians and left Egypt and came to Palestine and inhabited what is now called Judea. For the Hebrews had a paternal dialect before their descent into Egypt, and there were Hebrew letters, different from those of the Egyptians, which Moses, having used, wrote the five holy books believed by the Jews to be from them.
pass_b_english: Celsus, then, never became a fair examiner of what Egyptians say on one hand and Hebrews on the other; instead, he was prepossessed, as if by partisans of the Egyptians. To those who wronged the foreigners he assented as if they spoke truth, while he claimed that the wronged Hebrews, who were rebelling, left Egypt — failing to see how a rebellious multitude of Egyptians that large could not have come into existence, taking the rebellion as its beginning, becoming a nation at the same time as it rebelled, and changing its dialect so that those who until then had been using the Egyptian tongue might suddenly adopt the Hebrew one. Let us grant, for the sake of hypothesis, that they left Egypt hating both it and its native speech; how then did they not rather use the Syrian dialect afterward, or the Phoenician, but instead established the Hebrew dialect, distinct from both? This is what my argument aims to show: that it is false that some Egyptians, being of that stock, rebelled against Egyptians, left Egypt, came to Palestine, and settled in what is now called Judea. For the Hebrews possessed a paternal dialect before their descent into Egypt, and there were Hebrew letters, different from Egyptian ones, which Moses used to write the five holy books believed by the Jews.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex syntax of the Greek, particularly the conditional/hypothetical structure and the argument regarding the origin of the Hebrew dialect. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.
